mkdir -p $SCRATCH/eg/cmd/profharness && cat > $SCRATCH/eg/cmd/profharness/main.go <<'EOF'
package main

import (
	"context"
	"flag"
	"fmt"
	"os"
	"runtime"
	"runtime/pprof"
	"time"

	"github.com/entireio/entire-graph/internal/sem"
)

func main() {
	repo := flag.String("repo", ".", "repo")
	profile := flag.String("profile", "full", "profile")
	cpuOut := flag.String("cpu", "", "cpu profile out")
	memOut := flag.String("mem", "", "alloc profile out")
	worktree := flag.Bool("worktree", false, "worktree")
	flag.Parse()

	if *cpuOut != "" {
		f, err := os.Create(*cpuOut)
		if err != nil {
			panic(err)
		}
		pprof.StartCPUProfile(f)
		defer pprof.StopCPUProfile()
	}

	var m0, m1 runtime.MemStats
	runtime.ReadMemStats(&m0)
	start := time.Now()

	records := 0
	err := sem.StreamSnapshot(context.Background(), *repo, "prof", sem.ProviderSnapshotOptions{
		NoNetwork: true,
		Worktree:  *worktree,
		Profile:   sem.Profile(*profile),
	}, func(record any) error {
		records++
		return nil
	})
	elapsed := time.Since(start)
	runtime.ReadMemStats(&m1)
	if err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "error:", err)
	}
	fmt.Printf("records=%d wall=%s totalAlloc=%.1fMiB mallocs=%d heapSys=%.1fMiB numGC=%d pauseTotal=%s\n",
		records, elapsed,
		float64(m1.TotalAlloc-m0.TotalAlloc)/(1<<20),
		m1.Mallocs-m0.Mallocs,
		float64(m1.HeapSys)/(1<<20),
		m1.NumGC-m0.NumGC,
		time.Duration(m1.PauseTotalNs-m0.PauseTotalNs))

	if *memOut != "" {
		f, err := os.Create(*memOut)
		if err != nil {
			panic(err)
		}
		pprof.Lookup("allocs").WriteTo(f, 0)
		f.Close()
	}
}
EOF

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in. Format is part of this read — decided, not defaulted: a Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title and takes almost none of the craft below, so it fits only when the user asked for Markdown or the content is bound for a Markdown-native destination; never pick it to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* — most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token — a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Before publishing, scan the stylesheet for any color declared only inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — that is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject — or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name — a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word — a greeting, a category, a page-type label — the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

Performance assessment entire-graph @ 9cdc0592 Measured 2026-09-04

Ninety-six percent of a snapshot runs in one goroutine.

Every measurement below comes from CPU and allocation profiles of the real provider over a real repository. Two findings dominate: the relation phase is entirely single-threaded on a 24-core machine, and 70% of all allocations are regular expressions being recompiled inside hot loops. The second one is already fixed and verified byte-for-byte.

The shape of a run

Where the wall clock goes

relations — 38.28s — 96.3% — 1 goroutine
inventory 0.14s parse 1.30s · 24 workers relations 38.28s · sequential finalize 0.5ms

The parse phase already runs through runProviderFilePipeline with a worker pool and a deterministic in-order reducer. It scales: 4.01s at one worker down to 0.96s at twenty-four. The relation phase — forEachRelation in internal/sem/provider.go:2810 — is a plain for _, file := range files loop. It carries 79.9% of total CPU samples and gets no parallelism at all.

Whole-process concurrency for a full snapshot is 1.17×. Twenty-three cores are effectively idle for the duration of the run.

Wall clock 39.7s Full snapshot, 1,376 Go files, 190,565 records emitted.
Total allocated 10.5 GiB 124.6M mallocs against a 182 MiB peak heap. Churn, not footprint.
Effective parallelism 1.17× 58.96s of CPU samples over 46.6s of wall on 24 cores.
Cold search latency 21.4s search --profile full, the first action AGENTS.md asks every agent to take.
The allocation profile

Seven of ten gigabytes are regex compilation

regexp.compile accounts for 7.22 GiB of the 10.35 GiB sampled — 69.8%. Every byte of it is a pattern that is a compile-time constant being recompiled per call. Two functions produce 86% of it.

Runtime regex compilation by caller — baseline alloc_space profile
Function Site Allocated Share of compile
forwardedParameterProperty types.go:1518 4,283 MiB 59.3%
parameterVarTypes types.go:3134 1,907 MiB 26.4%
branchAssignedReturnFlows types.go 315 MiB 4.4%
parameterPropertyAliasForwardingFlows types.go:1539 275 MiB 3.8%
callLikeIdentifiers provider.go 98 MiB 1.4%
goHTTPRouteRegistrations provider.go:20675 87 MiB 1.2%
All runtime compilation 7,224 MiB 69.8% of total allocs

forwardedParameterProperty compiles three constant patterns and is called once per argument, per call site, per symbol: 

func forwardedParameterProperty(arg string, params map[string]bool) (string, string, bool) {
	arg = strings.TrimPrefix(strings.TrimSpace(arg), "$")
	if match := regexp.MustCompile(`^([A-Za-z_$][\w$]*)\.([A-Za-z_$][\w$]*)$`).FindStringSubmatch(arg); ...
	if match := regexp.MustCompile(`^([A-Za-z_$][\w$]*)\[\s*(?:"([^"]+)"|'([^']+)'|([0-9]+))\s*\]$`) ...
	if match := regexp.MustCompile(`^([A-Za-z_$][\w$]*)\[\s*\]$`).FindStringSubmatch(arg); ...

Across internal/sem there are roughly 390 such sites with fully static patterns, plus 44 whose pattern is built per call from a symbol name and needs a small compiled-pattern cache rather than a package var.

Verified

What hoisting the constants actually bought

I applied the change in a scratch copy and re-ran the same snapshot. Output is byte-identical — both builds produce sha256 b7cb2c19… over the full NDJSON stream.

Full snapshot — entireio/cli @ 51d062a34, mean of two consecutive runs
Build Wall Total alloc Mallocs GC cycles GC pause
Baseline 40.3s 10,507 MiB 124.6M 348 31.0ms
Two functions hoisted 35.8s  −11% 4,275 MiB  −59% 49.6M  −60% 236 21.9ms
All static patterns hoisted 34.4s  −15% 3,260 MiB  −69% 39.8M  −68% 204 19.6ms

Six lines of code in two functions recover 59% of the allocation churn and most of the wall-clock gain. The remaining ~390 sites add another ten points of allocation reduction for mechanical, reviewable work.

The interactive path

A search re-parses /proc/self/mountinfo 24,948 times

openSameVolumePath, lstatSameVolumePath and readlinkSameVolumePath each construct a fresh newSameVolumePathResolver, and every resolver calls newPathMountGuard, which reads and parses the whole mount table. Those helpers are called per path during the nested-.git directory walk, which itself runs during both preselection and the snapshot build.

I counted the calls with an instrumented build: 24,948 full parses of /proc/self/mountinfo in one search invocation, costing 2.87s of 17.4s CPU. The codebase already has the right pattern nearby — sweepDirectoryRoot.loadMountPoints guards the same read with a sync.Once.

Cold worktree search — query "resolve checkpoint trailer from commit"
Build Wall (fast) Wall (full) Alloc (fast) Mountinfo parses
Baseline 9.99s 21.4s 4,429 MiB 24,948
+ regex hoisting 9.85s — 4,386 MiB 24,948
+ mount-table reuse 7.70s  −23% 17.1s  −20% 3,714 MiB  −16% 1

Scope this one carefully. The guard exists to snapshot the mount table before resolving a repository-controlled path, so an autofs or remote mount cannot be activated just to discover it is on another device. A process-lifetime cache weakens that. Scope the reuse to one command — one snapshot build, one search — the way sweepDirectoryRoot already scopes it to one root, and the security property holds while the 24,947 redundant parses go away.

Ranked by measured payoff

What to do

01

Parallelize the relation phase

Projected

Give forEachRelation's per-file loop the same treatment the parse phase already has: a worker pool producing per-file results, and a sequential reducer consuming them in path order so streaming stays deterministic. The prologue that builds the shared indexes stays sequential; the loop body only reads them. In the ~950-line body there are only five writes to outer scope — resolvedImportsByFile, routeHandlers, handledRoutes, httpCallsByRoute and inheritanceEdges — all append-shaped and all reducible.

The parse phase reaches 4.2× on 24 workers, limited by its reducer and I/O. The relation phase has ~7× more parallel work per file against a comparably cheap reducer, so its Amdahl ceiling is far higher; 6–10× is a realistic band before GC and memory bandwidth bite.

relations 33.7s → 4–6s full snapshot 34.4s → 6–9s cold search full 17.1s → ~6s
02

Hoist constant regexes to package vars

Measured

Start with forwardedParameterProperty and parameterVarTypes: six patterns, and 59% of the churn. Then sweep the rest of internal/sem. For the 44 sites whose pattern is built per call (regexp.QuoteMeta(name) and friends, mostly in typescript.go, kotlin.go and the route scanners), add a small bounded compiled-pattern cache instead — or restructure to a static pattern plus a post-match name comparison, which is cheaper still.

A go vet-style check or a lint rule banning regexp.MustCompile inside function bodies would keep it from coming back.

allocations −69% mallocs −68% wall −15% output byte-identical
03

Reuse one mount-table snapshot per command

Measured

Thread a single resolver through the gitDirExcluder walk instead of constructing one per path, or memoize the mount snapshot for the lifetime of one operation. Biggest single win on the interactive path, which is the one agents actually wait on.

search fast −23% search full −20% allocations −16%
04

Compute per-body derivations once

Projected

Several scanners recompute the same thing from the same text. stripCodeLiteralsAndComments is called by nineteen different functions on the same body and allocates 529 MiB doing it. parameterAliasMap costs 3.15s of CPU and is called five times per body from five sibling forwarding-flow scanners. staticStringConstants costs 3.27s, and half of that is goHTTPRouteRegistrations recomputing a map the caller already has in fileStringConstants.

The clean shape is a per-symbol derived-context struct built once and passed down, rather than each scanner re-deriving from the raw body. It also removes the shared mutable state that a naive memo would introduce right before you parallelize.

relation-phase CPU −10–15% allocations −0.5 GiB
05

Gate the whole-repo route passes on language presence

Latent

Eight route-extraction passes each iterate every file in the repository. Five check the extension first and cost nothing on a repo without that language. Three — djangoRouteRelations, laravelRouteRelations and railsRouteRelations — build whole-repo indexes before any language check, and the last two do it with a nested loop over the symbols in each file. The language set is already computed in phase 1; gating on it is a two-line change.

Below the profiler's threshold on this repository, so this is a scaling hazard rather than a current cost — it grows with symbol density, not with the language actually being present.

current cost <0.2s risk quadratic in symbols/file
06

Revisit GOGC after parallelizing, not before

Measured

Today GOGC=400 buys about 3% of wall clock and costs 210 MiB of heap, because background marking runs on cores the single-threaded relation phase is not using. Once that phase is parallel, GC assists will compete for real work and the trade changes. Worth re-measuring then; not worth shipping now.

GOGC=100 38.0s / 186 MiB GOGC=400 36.8s / 394 MiB GOGC=800 37.1s / 667 MiB
Reproducing this

Method and caveats

Target. github.com/entireio/cli at 51d062a34 — 1,589 tracked files, 1,376 of them Go, 190,565 snapshot records. Machine: 24 cores, Linux, Go 1.26.7. Profiles taken through sem.StreamSnapshot and sem.SearchRepository directly, with a no-op emit sink; the real CLI adds under 0.5s for NDJSON encoding (35.7s vs 35.3s), so encoding is not a factor.

content.text:
All four are implemented in the working tree. Updated report: **https://claude.ai/code/artifact/39cbb0e3-472a-4def-aae5-d0008dc653d5**

**Results** on `entireio/cli` (1,376 Go files, 190,565 records), mean of two runs on an idle machine:

| | before | after | |
|---|---|---|---|
| full snapshot | 40.1s | **14.2s** | −65% (2.8×) |
| total alloc | 10,507 MiB | **2,915 MiB** | −72% |
| mallocs | 124.6M | **39.4M** | −68% |
| relations phase | 38.3s | **12.9s** | −66% |
| search `--profile full` | 20.9s | **9.3s** | −55% |
| search `fast` | 9.5s | **6.6s** | −31% |

**What changed**

1. **Parallel relation phase.** Generalized `runProviderFilePipeline` into `runIndexedPipeline[T]`, so both phases share one coordinator. The loop body became a per-file closure that shadows `emit`/`recordFailure` to buffer, and a reducer replays relations, failures and the four accumulators in file order. The body had only four writes to enclosing scope, all append-shaped, and no cross-iteration reads. Two memoizing closures (`jsCrossFileNamespaceLookup`, `pythonModuleExists`) needed mutexes.

2. **Regex hoisting.** An AST rewriter moved all **180** in-function literal `regexp.MustCompile` calls to package vars next to their function, then a second pass removed the 88 `local := packageVar` aliases it left. The nine identical call-site patterns collapsed into one `flowCallSiteRe`. `TestRegexpLiteralsAreCompiledOnce` fails on any new one; patterns built per call from a symbol name are correctly out of scope.

3. **Mount-table reuse.** `mountTableCache` serves one snapshot per operation, taken at `streamSnapshotWithWorkerCount` and `searchRepository` entry — before anything repository-controlled is resolved, which is the ordering the guard depends on. Failed reads are deliberately not cached. 24,948 parses of `/proc/self/mountinfo` per search → 1.

4. **Per-body derivations.** A `symbolBody` value carries the stripped copy through 16 scanners (was 16 strips per symbol); `parameterAliasMap` computed once in `returnFlowCalls` instead of 5×; a `fileStringConstants` cache shared between the route pass and the per-file loop.

**Verification.** Byte-identical NDJSON across 4 repos × `full`/`fast`/`syntax-only` × committed/worktree — every pair matches. Race detector clean on a full 1,376-file snapshot. Worker-count determinism, emission-ordering, golden-fixture, compact round-trip and the new tests pass.

Two things you should know:

- **I could not run the full suite.** No C++ compiler here, so I build and test in mirrors with the YAML tree-sitter grammar stubbed. Three tests fail from that stub — and fail identically on the unmodified tree. newSameVolumePathResolver read and parsed the whole platform mount table

/proc/self/mountinfo 24,948 times and spent 2.9 of 9.4 seconds doing it.

Provider operations declare the boundary as they start, which is the
point before which nothing repository-controlled has been resolved, so
the ordering pathMountGuard depends on is preserved: the table is still
read before any untrusted path is. Sharing cannot widen what a resolver
accepts either, because the table only decides whether a candidate is
looked at at all, and every hop that survives it is still device-checked
against the base by pathTraversalAnchor.allows.

What it gives up is freshness inside one operation: a mount created
after the snapshot is absent from it, so its trigger point can be looked
at once. The device check still refuses to cross it.

A failed read is deliberately not cached. Remembering it would let one
transient failure refuse every path for the rest of the operation, where
the per-resolver read this replaces simply tried again on the next path.

The win is on the query path, which resolves far more paths than a
committed-tree snapshot does. Cold worktree search of entireio/cli, fast
profile: 9.45s -> 7.45s wall and 4,433 MiB -> 3,765 MiB allocated, with
